arXiv:2505.01479v1 [cs.CL] 02 May 2025

SymPlanner: Deliberate Planning in Language Models with
Symbolic Representation

Siheng Xiong    Jieyu Zhou    Zhangding Liu    Yusen Su Affiliation: Georgia Institute of Technology Affiliation: {sxiong45, jzhou625, zliu952, ysu349}@gatech.edu
Abstract

Planning remains a core challenge for language models (LMs), particularly in domains that require coherent multi-step action sequences grounded in external constraints. We introduce SymPlanner, a novel framework that equips LMs with structured planning capabilities by interfacing them with a symbolic environment that serves as an explicit world model. Rather than relying purely on natural language reasoning, SymPlanner grounds the planning process in a symbolic state space, where a policy model proposes actions and a symbolic environment deterministically executes and verifies their effects. To enhance exploration and improve robustness, we introduce Iterative Correction (IC), which refines previously proposed actions by leveraging feedback from the symbolic environment to eliminate invalid decisions and guide the model toward valid alternatives. Additionally, Contrastive Ranking (CR) enables fine-grained comparison of candidate plans by evaluating them jointly. We evaluate SymPlanner on PlanBench, demonstrating that it produces more coherent, diverse, and verifiable plans than pure natural language baselines.11 1 Code and data are available at https://github.com/xiongsiheng/SymPlanner.

1 Introduction

Planning is a fundamental aspect of intelligent behavior, involving the construction of coherent action sequences to achieve specific goals. In real-world applications, such as robotics, virtual agents, and interactive assistants Jiang et al. (2024b); Jin et al. (2024); Liu et al. (2025), effective planning requires not only long-horizon decision-making but also strict adherence to external constraints and logical consistency. While large language models (LMs) have demonstrated strong reasoning capabilities, they continue to struggle in planning tasks where actions must be grounded in a verifiable and coherent world model Valmeekam et al. (2023). These challenges are particularly evident in domains that demand structured, multi-step decision-making under rigid task rules.

Existing LM-based approaches, e.g., Chain-of-Thought (COT) Wei et al. (2022), Tree-of-Thought (TOT) Yao et al. (2023), Reasoning-as-Planning (RAP) Hao et al. (2023), reason/plan predominantly rely on natural language to represent both states and actions. Although this paradigm offers simplicity and flexibility, it lacks the structural rigor necessary for reliable execution. Without an explicit environment to validate decisions, natural language-based reasoning often yields plans that are inconsistent or violate domain-specific constraints—especially as task complexity increases Yang et al. (2024). This stems from the ambiguity of natural language Jiang et al. (2024a) and the lack of grounding in a deterministic state space.

To overcome these limitations, we propose SymPlanner, a novel framework that augments language models with structured planning capabilities by interfacing them with a symbolic environment. This environment acts as an explicit and deterministic world model, allowing the LM to anchor its decisions in a structured, verifiable state space. A policy model generates candidate actions, which are executed and validated by the symbolic environment. When invalid actions are detected, the model revises them through an Iterative Correction (IC) mechanism that incorporates feedback. To further enhance plan quality, we introduce Contrastive Ranking (CR), enabling fine-grained comparisons among multiple candidates. These mechanisms collectively enhance planning accuracy, coherence, and diversity. We evaluate SymPlanner on PlanBench, demonstrating substantial improvements over natural language-only baselines in terms of plan validity, coherence, and diversity.

Specifically, our main contributions include:

  • •

    We introduce SymPlanner, a framework that couples language models with a symbolic environment to enable structured and verifiable planning.

  • •

    We propose Iterative Correction, a feedback-driven refinement process for invalid actions, and Contrastive Ranking, a technique for selecting the most coherent plan among candidates.

  • •

    We validate our approach on PlanBench, showing that SymPlanner outperforms natural language-only baselines in both planning robustness and execution fidelity.

2 Methodology

In this section, we present our framework (SymPlanner) that equips LMs with structured planning capabilities by interfacing them with a symbolic environment that serves as an explicit world model. We use 𝒫π{\mathcal{P}}_{\pi} to denote the policy, 𝒫d{\mathcal{P}}_{\text{d}} to denote the discriminator, both based on pre-trained LMs, and ℳwm{\mathcal{M}}_{\text{wm}} to denote the symbolic world model. We consider g,s,ag,s,a as language sequences, i.e., g=(g⁡[1],⋯,g⁡[L])g=(g[1],\cdots,g[L]) where each g⁡[l]g[l] is a token, so that 𝒫(g)=∏l=1L𝒫(g[l]|g[1..l−1]){\mathcal{P}}(g)=\prod_{l=1}^{L}{\mathcal{P}}(g[l]|g{[1..l-1]}). We use gg to denote the goal, ss to denote the state, aa to denote the action, and Π=[a1,…,at−1]\Pi=[a_{1},\dots,a_{t-1}] is the list of actions, i.e., the plan.

For notational convenience, we define the generation process as gen​(model,input,N)\texttt{gen}(\texttt{model},\texttt{input},N) where NN is the number of generations, and the discrimination process as dis​(model,input,b)\texttt{dis}(\texttt{model},\texttt{input},b) where bb is the number of preserved candidates. To compare potential actions, we simulate the possible future states of each candidate action using the symbolic world model, which is denoted by st=symSim​(g,s,a,t)s_{t}=\texttt{symSim}(g,s,a,t) given goal gg, state ss, action aa and target step tt.

Algorithm 1 outlines the workflow. Given a goal gg and current state st−1s_{t-1}, the policy proposes a set of actions ata_{t} by sampling NN times from 𝒫π​(a|g,s){\mathcal{P}}_{\pi}(a|g,s). The top bb candidate actions are selected by the discriminator 𝒫d{\mathcal{P}}_{\text{d}} based on the simulation results sTs_{T}. The state prediction is then performed in parallel for each selected action (st−1s_{t-1}, ata_{t}) by the symbolic world model. Based on the generated sts_{t}, the policy determines whether to continue reasoning. If the goal is achieved, the policy stores the plan Π\Pi in the completed pool 𝒟\mathcal{D}, and reduces the rollout budget bb by 1. Otherwise, (g,st,Πt)(g,s_{t},\Pi_{t}) will be added to the unfinished pool 𝒞\mathcal{C} for the next step. The process continues until the step limit TT is reached or bb becomes 0. Finally, the top plan Π∗\Pi^{*} is selected by the discriminator 𝒫d{\mathcal{P}}_{\text{d}} from the completed pool 𝒟\mathcal{D}.

To further enhance the system, we incorporate iterative correction and contrastive ranking. The key idea is to leverage feedback from the symbolic world model to guide the policy model in refining its actions. This external feedback helps mitigate the model’s inherent biases and improves decision quality Tong et al. (2024); Xu et al. (2024). Additionally, rather than evaluating each option independently, the discriminator compares multiple options simultaneously. This contrastive comparison enables the model to better capture subtle differences between options, resulting in more stable and informative reward signals (Xiong et al., 2024b). We conduct an ablation study to empirically validate the effectiveness of these components within our framework.

3 Experiments

3.1 Experimental setup

In this section, we demonstrate the versatility and effectiveness of our framework by applying it to PlanBench Valmeekam et al. (2023), where a robotic agent manipulates blocks on a table to achieve a goal configuration. We formalize planning as a sequence of symbolic operations (Pickup, Putdown, Stack, and Unstack) parsed by LMs Yang et al. (2023). The key parameter settings used in SymPlanner are as follows: the maximum number of planning steps is set to 16; each planning instance involves 32 rollouts; the generation process consists of 3 iterations; and both the group size and beam width are set to 3. For contrastive ranking, each option is compared against one alternative (i.e., one comparison per option).

We evaluate SymPlanner against several popular reasoning strategies, including Zero/Few-shot CoT, ToT, and RAP from the LLM Reasoners library (Hao et al., 2024), and employ verification with a symbolic validator (Howey et al., 2004). We conduct experiments using three different base models: GPT-4o-mini, GPT-4o and GPT-4.1. Implementation settings are as follows: CoT draws independent reasoning chains for each example at a sampling temperature of 0. ToT is configured with a generation limit of 4, a breadth limit of 4, and a search depth cap of 6, resulting in 32 total rollouts. RAP is configured with a planning depth limit of 6, a cumulative reward function, and mean-based Q-value estimation. MCTS is adopted as the search strategy, and symbolic feedback is incorporated via external model. The temperature for all the planning methods (ToT, RAP, SymPlanner) is fixed at 0.7. To balance evaluation quality and computational cost, we randomly sample 20 test instances for each step count.

3.2 Main results

Table 1 reports the accuracy across different step counts for GPT-4o-mini, GPT-4o, and GPT-4.1. SymPlanner consistently achieves the highest total accuracy, with gains becoming more pronounced on larger models (50.0% on GPT-4o and 54.2% on GPT-4.1, compared to 21.6% on GPT-4o-mini), suggesting effective scaling with model capacity. While baseline methods (Zero-shot CoT, Few-shot CoT, ToT, and RAP) degrade sharply as step counts increase (often failing beyond four steps), SymPlanner maintains competitive performance across longer horizons (e.g., 55.0% and 50.0% at 8 steps). These results highlight SymPlanner’s robustness against error accumulation and its superior handling of complex, multi-step reasoning.

For baselines, few-shot CoT consistently outperforms zero-shot CoT, confirming the value of providing demonstration examples. However, even with 4-shot prompting, few-shot CoT lags significantly behind SymPlanner, especially at higher step counts, suggesting that prompting improvements alone are insufficient for overcoming the challenges of long-horizon reasoning. Finally, RAP achieves high accuracy at short step counts but fails to generalize to longer chains, highlighting a key limitation of methods that emphasize local improvement without global planning. In contrast, SymPlanner’s sustained performance across varying step counts suggests better planning and goal-directed reasoning throughout the sequence. Overall, the results demonstrate that SymPlanner not only improves single-step decision quality but also offers significant advantages in maintaining reasoning coherence over longer trajectories, particularly when paired with stronger base models.

3.3 Ablation study

We analyze the impact of key components in our framework (Table 2). The complete method achieves the highest overall accuracy of 54.2%, confirming that each component contributes positively. Removing the symbolic representation causes a substantial drop to 46.7%, indicating its importance in providing reliable state information. Ablating iterative correction leads to a sharper decline in performance to 20.8%, especially at higher step counts, highlighting its critical role in mitigating error accumulation. Removing contrastive ranking yields a moderate decrease to 27.5%, with a more pronounced impact on mid-range difficulties. These results collectively demonstrate that symbolic representation, iterative correction, and contrastive ranking are all vital for achieving robust and scalable multi-step reasoning.

4 Related Work

LM-based planning systems enhance planning accuracy by incorporating environmental state information, either obtained directly from the environment or predicted by LMs. Systems that access states directly typically build skill memory through trial-and-error learning, but most focus on short-horizon tasks and provide feedback only after task completion Zhu et al. (2023); Wang et al. (2023b); Wang et al. (2023a). In contrast, our method addresses longer multi-step tasks, where early errors can propagate and lead to overall failure. By iteratively correcting each generated step, our system filters out invalid actions and significantly improves success rates. Compared to approaches that rely on LLMs for step-by-step state prediction Yao et al. (2022); Hao et al. (2023), which are prone to compounding errors, SymPlanner leverages direct symbolic environment feedback for greater reliability. In neural-symbolic planning systems, two policy strategies are commonly used: goal alignment and effect alignment. For example, Kirk et al. (2024) propose a goal-alignment strategy to evaluate candidate actions generated by LLMs. Future work could explore integrating goal-alignment policies directly into discriminators for further improvements.

We also explored test-time compute with process reward models (PRMs) Lightman et al. (2023); Li et al. (2024), which assess intermediate steps to better support multi-step planning/reasoning but face challenges related to scalable supervision and score calibration Luo et al. (2024). To address these limitations, we propose Contrastive Ranking (CR), which directly compares candidate options within prompts, leading to improved discrimination accuracy. Enhancing LMs with symbolic representations Xiong et al. (2024a); Liu et al. (2024); Yu et al. (2024); Ni et al. (2024) is a promising direction. These representations not only improve interpretability but also serve as a structured interface for integrating external knowledge sources and verifying model outputs He et al. (2023); He et al. (2024). In SymPlanner, symbolic feedback acts as a robust grounding mechanism that helps mitigate the cascading failure issue in long-horizon planning. Additionally, semantic equivalence checks allow us to filter redundant or invalid reasoning paths, thereby preserving diversity without sacrificing correctness.

5 Conclusion

We introduce SymPlanner, a deliberate planning framework that augments language models with a symbolic environment to enhance planning performance. By incorporating iterative correction and contrastive ranking, SymPlanner achieves strong results on PlanBench. Looking ahead, integrating reinforcement learning presents a promising direction to further improve the robustness and adaptability of our framework in real-world tasks. By using symbolic feedback as a reward signal and adopting a process-aware exploration strategy, future extensions of SymPlanner could autonomously learn to generate efficient and correct action sequences in more complex environments.

Appendix A Prompts

In this section, we present all the prompts used in our framework. These prompts include those for action and state generation, action parsing, iterative correction, plan rating, and contrastive ranking.

Appendix B Dataset Overview

PlanBench Valmeekam et al. (2023) is a benchmark, including various planning tasks such as plan generation, optimal planning, plan verification, plan reuse, plan generalization, replanning, reasoning about plan execution, and goal reformulation. In our work, we primarily focus on the task of plan generation and use a symbolic verifier for validating generated plans. The dataset contains 600 instances, each consisting of an initial state (e.g., "The orange block is clear, the red block is clear, the hand is empty, the orange block is on the blue block, the blue block is on the table, the red block is on the table") and a goal state (e.g., "The blue block is on the orange block"). The action space includes four types: Pick up a block, Unstack a block from on top of another block, Put down a block, and Stack a block on top of another block, each with well-defined preconditions and effects. Based on the number of steps in the reference plan, the instances are categorized into six difficulty levels: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, and 12 steps. We report performance results for each category in our experiments.
